threats.name: Late blight
threats.description: A fungal disease that spreads at mild temperatures when the leaf stays wet, leaving dark spots with a pale edge and a firm brown rot on the fruit.
prevention: Water at the root only, never over the leaves.
Pinch out side shoots and lower leaves so air can move through.
Space plants far enough apart that leaves dry quickly after rain.
Rotate with at least a three-year gap.
response: Remove diseased leaves and take them out of the garden.
Spray with an approved copper preparation or horsetail tea.
Stop overhead watering and improve ventilation.
Pick healthy fruit before the infection advances.

threats.name: Early blight
threats.description: Dark concentric spots on older leaves that spread upward, favoured by warm weather where the leaf repeatedly wets and dries.
prevention: Mulch the soil so rain cannot splash it onto the lower leaves.
Keep nitrogen feeding balanced.
Clear and destroy plant debris after harvest.
response: Strip the oldest infected leaves.
Treat with an approved copper preparation.
Water in the morning so leaves go into the night dry.

threats.name: Tomato leafminer
threats.description: Larvae mine the leaves and bore into the fruit, with generations following each other faster as it gets warmer.
prevention: Pheromone traps to track the flight.
Remove and destroy attacked fruit and leaves.
Insect netting over greenhouse openings.
response: Set pheromone traps densely for mass trapping.
Use Bacillus thuringiensis preparations while larvae are young.
Strip mined leaves before the larvae move into the fruit.

threats.name: Blossom-end rot
threats.description: A physiological disorder rather than a disease: in heat with uneven watering the plant cannot move calcium to the fruit, so its tip darkens and collapses. It does not spread from plant to plant.
prevention: Water evenly, without sudden dry spells.
Mulch to hold moisture in the soil.
Avoid overdoing nitrogen fertiliser.
response: Return to a steady rhythm of smaller, regular waterings.
Mulch straight away to cut evaporation.
Pick off affected fruit so the plant stops spending on it.

threats.name: Potato late blight
threats.description: The most damaging potato disease: in wet weather it can destroy the whole haulm within days, and spores wash from the leaves down to the tubers.
prevention: Certified, healthy seed potatoes.
Earth up high so spores cannot reach the tubers.
Rotate crops and destroy volunteer plants.
Apply preventive copper ahead of a forecast wet spell.
response: Spray with approved copper preparations.
Treat with horsetail tea.
Cut and remove the haulm in a heavy infection, two weeks before lifting.
Lift the tubers in dry weather.

threats.name: Early blight
threats.description: Dry leaf spotting with concentric rings, appearing in warmer weather and on plants weakening towards the end of the season.
prevention: Balanced feeding, since weakened plants go down first.
Mulch the soil under the plants.
Clear plant debris after lifting.
response: Remove the oldest infected leaves.
Treat with an approved copper preparation.
Feed the crop to strengthen it.

threats.name: Colorado potato beetle
threats.description: Adults and larvae strip the leaves to the veins; in warm dry weather development speeds up and generations overlap.
prevention: Rotate, putting the plot as far as possible from last year's.
Plant early to dodge the heaviest attack.
Check leaf undersides regularly and crush egg clusters.
response: Hand-pick adults and egg clusters.
Use Bacillus thuringiensis var. tenebrionis while larvae are young.
Remove badly stripped haulm.

threats.name: Tuber cracking
threats.description: A heavy downpour after a dry spell forces the tuber into sudden growth, so it splits or throws out knobs. Cracked tubers do not store.
prevention: Water evenly while the tubers are forming.
Mulch and earth up to keep soil moisture steadier.
response: Bring watering back gradually rather than in one large dose.
Lift in dry weather and sort cracked tubers out before storing.

threats.name: Cucumber downy mildew
threats.description: Angular yellow patches bounded by the leaf veins, with a grey bloom underneath; in wet weather a crop can be lost within a week.
prevention: Grow on a trellis so leaves dry faster.
Avoid wetting the foliage when watering.
Leave enough space between plants.
response: Stop overhead watering and switch to the root.
Treat with an approved copper preparation.
Remove the first infected leaves and take them out of the garden.

threats.name: Powdery mildew
threats.description: A white, flour-like coating on the upper leaf surface. Unlike downy mildew it wants warmth and humid air but a dry leaf, so it appears even without rain.
prevention: Space plants and strip lower leaves so air can flow.
Avoid excess nitrogen.
Choose tolerant varieties.
response: Spray a baking soda solution with a few drops of vegetable oil.
Apply an approved sulphur preparation on a cloudy day, never in heat.
Pull off the worst-affected lower leaves.

threats.name: Two-spotted spider mite
threats.description: A tiny mite on the leaf underside; in hot dry weather it multiplies explosively, leaving the leaf stippled, grey and finally dead.
prevention: Check leaf undersides regularly — an attack is usually noticed late.
Keep humidity up around the plants during the hottest spells.
Clear weeds that host the mite.
response: Hose the leaf undersides hard with water to break up the population.
Use plant-oil or potassium-soap preparations.
Remove and destroy the worst-affected leaves.

threats.name: Fruit bitterness
threats.description: In heat and water shortage the plant produces cucurbitacins and the fruit turns bitter. It is not a disease, does not spread, and no spray will fix it.
prevention: Water regularly with no dry gaps.
Mulch and shade through the hottest days.
response: Get back to regular watering.
Pick more often, while the fruit is younger and smaller.

threats.name: Cabbage downy mildew
threats.description: Yellowish patches on the upper leaf with a white bloom beneath; most dangerous on seedlings and young plants in cool wet weather.
prevention: Do not plant where other brassicas grew last year.
Space plants so air can move through.
Water in the morning so leaves go into the night dry.
response: Treat with chamomile or horsetail tea.
Dust wood ash around the plants.
Collect infected leaves and destroy them away from the garden.

threats.name: Black rot
threats.description: A bacterial disease, not a fungal one, which is why copper does little against it. It shows as yellow V-shaped patches with blackened veins, in warm rainy weather.
prevention: Healthy certified transplants from a trusted source.
A rotation of at least four years without brassicas.
Never work in the crop while the plants are wet.
response: Pull and destroy diseased plants away from the garden.
Stop all work in a wet crop — hands and tools carry the bacterium.
Improve drainage and stop watering over the leaves.

threats.name: Large white butterfly
threats.description: The caterpillars chew leaves down to the veins and bore into the head. The butterfly flies most in warm dry weather.
prevention: Insect netting over the crop from planting.
Check leaf undersides regularly and remove egg clusters.
Plant aromatic companions that put the butterfly off.
response: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters.
Use Bacillus thuringiensis while the caterpillars are young.
Remove the worst-chewed leaves.

threats.name: Head splitting
threats.description: Heavy rain after a dry spell fills the head with water and it splits; rot enters through the crack immediately.
prevention: Water evenly as the heads approach maturity.
Cut mature heads promptly.
response: Cut mature heads before forecast rain arrives.
Give over-mature heads a slight root twist to slow water uptake.

threats.name: Onion downy mildew
threats.description: Pale elongated patches with a violet bloom on a damp morning; the leaf folds over and the bulb stays small.
prevention: Preventive copper in wet periods.
Avoid excess nitrogen, which gives soft susceptible leaves.
Rotate and remove volunteer onions.
response: Apply approved copper preparations without delay.
Spray with horsetail tea.
Break the soil crust shallowly so the ground dries faster.

threats.name: Purple blotch
threats.description: Oval spots with a purple centre on older leaves, appearing in the warmer part of the season, often after damage from mildew or thrips.
prevention: Remove older damaged leaves.
Rotate and plough residues in deeply.
Control thrips, whose wounds let the fungus in.
response: Treat with an approved copper preparation.
Strip badly affected leaves.
Stop watering over the foliage.

threats.name: Onion fly
threats.description: Larvae bore into the bulb, the plant yellows and wilts, and the bulb rots. The first flight is in spring, at mild temperatures with damp soil.
prevention: Insect netting immediately after sowing.
Rotate and keep distance from last year's plot.
Avoid fresh manure, which attracts the fly.
response: Pull and destroy attacked plants together with the larvae.
Dust wood ash or rock flour around the plants.
Drench with entomopathogenic nematodes.

threats.name: Waterlogging rot
threats.description: Water standing around the bulb for long causes rot and stops it ripening. The problem is the soil and its drainage, not a pathogen.
prevention: Plant on raised beds on heavy soils.
Stop watering towards the end of the season.
response: Drain the excess away through shallow channels at once.
Stop watering entirely.
Lift the onions as soon as weather allows and dry them thinly, in a draught.
